note: Regulatory and network layer for Canadian bank cards. Each rule carries its source and the date it was checked. flag:true means the figure could not be verified against a primary source and must be treated as directional. Full brief with exact wording: research/canada-card-rules.md.

mustKnow.rule: Maximum liability for unauthorised credit-card use, unless the bank proves gross negligence (gross fault in Quebec).
mustKnow.clientLine: For charges before you reported it, the law caps what you could owe at fifty dollars, and the bank would have to prove you were grossly careless to charge even that.

mustKnow.rule: No liability for any unauthorised use after the client reports the card, account information or PIN lost, stolen or at risk. A PIN having been used does not by itself establish negligence.
mustKnow.source: Bank Act s. 627.33(2) and (3); FCAC Bulletin B-6
mustKnow.clientLine: From this moment, nothing further can be charged to you.

mustKnow.rule: Maximum time for the PIN issuer to respond to a reported unauthorised debit transaction; may pause while a signed statement or affidavit is awaited. The issuer must prove the client contributed, on the balance of probabilities.
mustKnow.source: Canadian Code of Practice for Consumer Debit Card Services s. 6 (revised 2004)
mustKnow.clientLine: On a debit claim the bank has ten business days to respond to you.

mustKnow.rule: Visa and Mastercard cardholder dispute window, from the transaction date or the expected delivery date.
mustKnow.source: Visa Dispute Management Guidelines for Merchants, June 2024; Mastercard via acquirer documentation
mustKnow.flagReason: Mastercard's own Chargeback Guide was not fetchable; the 120-day figure comes from acquirer documentation that agrees across sources.
mustKnow.clientLine: You have up to 120 days from the purchase, or from when the goods were due, to dispute it, so we are inside the window.

mustKnow.rule: Legislated period for the bank to resolve or close a complaint. It cannot be paused.
mustKnow.source: FCPF Regulations SOR/2021-181 s. 14; FCAC guideline
mustKnow.clientLine: You will have our written decision within the 56-day period, which runs from the day you first raised this.

mustKnow.rule: An unresolved complaint must reach a Designated Employee within 14 days of first being received; the client may ask to escalate sooner.
mustKnow.source: FCAC Guideline on Complaint-Handling Procedures for Banks (2022, revised 2026-06-23)
mustKnow.clientLine: If I cannot resolve this, it goes to a designated complaints officer within fourteen days, and you can ask for that sooner.

mustKnow.rule: Window to go to OBSI after the final written response; maximum OBSI can recommend; OBSI's target for banking investigations. Recommendations are non-binding and refusals are published. Also available once 56 days have passed.
mustKnow.clientLine: If you disagree with our final answer, or 56 days pass, you can take it to OBSI free of charge within 180 days, and I will send you how.

mustKnow.rule: Minimum time from the end of a billing cycle to the minimum-payment due date; no interest on purchases if the full balance is paid by the due date. Cash advances, balance transfers and cash-like transactions get no grace period.
mustKnow.clientLine: Pay the full statement balance by the due date and there is no interest on purchases; a cash advance is different and charges interest from the day you take it.

mustKnow.figure: 7am to 9pm local; Sunday 1pm to 5pm; never on a holiday
mustKnow.rule: Permitted collection-contact hours without the debtor's written consent. No federal weekly call-count limit; that is provincial law for agencies.
Reported fraud losses in Canada in 2025. Bank investigator scam $37.4M in 2025 and $28.6M in the first half of 2026. CAFC estimates 5 to 10 percent of victims report.
mustKnow.source: CAFC Top 10 frauds 2025 (2026-02-25); CAFC H1 2026 trends (2026-08-25)
mustKnow.clientLine: This is a professional crime that cost Canadians over seven hundred million dollars last year; it works on careful people.

sections.title: Fraud versus merchant dispute
sections.summary: Unauthorised use is governed by the Bank Act cap, network zero liability, the Debit Code and FCAC B-6; the client blocks and reports, no merchant contact needed. An authorised charge that is wrong (not received, not as described, cancelled recurring, free-trial conversion) is a network chargeback: merchant first, evidence, 120-day window. Visa's stated position: a charge the cardholder expressly authorised 'is not fraud, so does not fall under Zero Liability'. Disputing a legitimate charge is friendly fraud and reverses against the client.

sections.title: Provisional credit
sections.summary: For credit cards, provisional credit is issuer policy, not law. Visa lists grounds to withhold, delay, limit or reverse it: gross negligence or fraud, delayed reporting, claim verification, account standing. Visa Debit: provisional credit 'within two business days' in most circumstances once the item has posted (from a search snippet; page not fetched).

sections.title: Complaint handling obligations
sections.summary: Any expression of dissatisfaction is a complaint and must be recorded for seven years. Written acknowledgement with the received date, the process, the timelines and the external body's details. Internal staff may not be called 'ombudsman'. Notice of Final Decision must state it concludes the internal process and give the OBSI route. OBSI was designated sole external complaints body on 2023-10-17 and assumed the role on 2024-11-01. FCAC's July 2025 review found banks failing to log every expression of dissatisfaction and missing the 56-day limit.

sections.title: Fees, interest and consent
sections.summary: No over-limit fee where the excess was caused by a merchant hold (s. 627.36). Credit-limit increases need express consent; using the card is not consent (s. 627.32); oral consent must be confirmed in writing. Payments above the minimum go to the highest-rate balance first or proportionally (s. 627.35). Merchants may surcharge credit cards up to 2.4 percent (not Quebec), must disclose before the transaction, and the client must be able to cancel without penalty.

sections.title: Seniors and vulnerable clients
sections.summary: CBA Seniors Code (2019): senior means 60 or over transacting for non-business purposes; Principle 5 obliges banks to mitigate financial harm from abuse, fraud or scams 'while respecting clients' privacy, and security and autonomy'; every bank has a Seniors Champion. PIPEDA s. 7(3)(d.3) permits disclosure without consent to a government institution or next of kin on reasonable grounds of financial abuse, solely to prevent or investigate it; the bank decides, the advisor escalates. Appropriate products (s. 627.06) apply even when the client asked for the product.

sections.title: Verification and third parties
sections.summary: Verify fully before disclosing anything, including whether an account exists. A spouse, parent or adult child has no right to account information unless joint holder, named authorised user within the agreement, or attorney under an accepted power of attorney. Marriage is not authority; a document described on a call is not authority until verified; the bank may require a copy of a POA before acting (OPC cases 2002-100, 2002-108, 2003-155, 2003-175, 2003-181, 2004-278). One-time codes are never requested from or relayed by a third party.

sections.title: The bank investigator scam
sections.summary: Automated call or spoofed number claiming to be the bank, police, a bureau or Amazon; asks for remote access, the one-time code 'to confirm identity', moving money to a 'safe account', or handing the card to a courier; may recite the card's first digits (the BIN). CAFC rules: never provide remote access, never share codes, institutions and police never ask for your card. Hang up and call the number on the back of the card. Recovery pitch follows: fraudsters impersonating the CAFC for a fee.
